title: Binance heist is stark example of AI governance gaps and basic security failures
raw_text: A chain of avoidable technical and human security failures enabled the largest crypto heist on record, the theft of approximately $6.34 billion from Binance . The improper monitoring and access scoping of an internal AI tool played a major role in helping the hackers, and should serve as a warning for enterprise CISOs to take AI governance seriously. Binance’s initial findings report , published Nov. 3, describes a months-long, multi-stage campaign against its wallet-infrastructure engineers that resulted in malware being installed on developer machines in two separate incidents, only one of which was detected. The attackers were then able to pivot through an internal AI tool to additional developer systems, obtain an access token, and deploy a container on Binance’s infrastructure before executing the rogue withdrawals. While Binance describes this attack as highly sophisticated, there were multiple security failures involved that could have been avoided, from weak or absent access controls to overly broad privileges, poor credential hygiene, and employee security awareness lapses or policy violations. “Developer workstations have quietly become some of the most privileged assets in the enterprise, carrying deployment tokens, signing access, and now AI tools that can act across internal systems on an employee’s behalf,” warns Joe Brinkley, director of offensive security research and community at security firm Cobalt. “Once an attacker controls that machine, an AI tool with broad internal reach becomes one more trusted path they can use.” He adds: “Security teams should treat engineers with production or signing access as a high-value attack surface, test the path from workstation to production the way an adversary would, and scope AI tool permissions as tightly as any service account.” Two compromises, months apart The FBI has attributed the Binance breach to North Korea , identifying the hacking unit as TraderTraitor, which other researchers consider part of the broader Lazarus operation that has stolen billions of dollars from cryptocurrency platforms over the past decade . Binance’s own report relays the FBI’s conclusion and notes that throughout 2026, the company’s security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea–linked cyber threat cases. This suggests Binance has the Lazarus APT in its threat model, as it should, and is well aware of the group’s tools, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), which include software supply-chain compromises, the use of malware that masquerades as popular legitimate tools, tricking developers with fake job interviews , and long-horizon social engineering operations. Yet, two Binance engineers fell victim to exactly these tricks, raising questions about the company’s security awareness training as well as its technical controls. In June, a wallet-infrastructure engineer searched the web for a popular AI coding tool and downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer rather than obtaining the software from a trusted source. Homebrew is a package manager and distribution channel for open-source applications on macOS. Binance’s security team detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials, but the attackers had already learned who the engineer was and who else worked on the wallet infrastructure team. It’s good that Binance was able to quickly detect the breach, but the incident raises the question of why an engineer was installing software from a search result at all. Does Binance have a policy that employees install software only from approved sources, and is this enforced with technical controls such as application whitelisting? Three months later, the attackers approached a second engineer through a job-hunting platform, posing as a project director recruiting for a company that did not exist. Two staged interviews followed: one with a purported HR representative who shared a social media account filled with personal photos and videos to build trust, and one with someone claiming to be the company’s CEO. At the end of the second interview, the engineer was told to download a coding assignment onto their work computer from a repository. The assignment included malicious code, and this time Binance’s endpoint protection tools did not detect it. The company described this as zero-day malware, but if endpoint protection tools were only capable of detecting known malware, then the whole industry has a problem. Either way, the developer’s actions raise a number of questions regarding security policies, procedures, and awareness at Binance, first among them: Why was the engineer doing job interviews and test assignments on their work computer? Why did they clone a repository directly on their system instead of using a virtual machine? If this is something they regularly do, then it points to lapses in security training or intentional policy violations. And companies cannot solely rely on employees always following policies. They need detection and enforcement mechanisms. “The engineer did multiple things wrong,” says Tim Chase, AVP for cybersecurity at human-risk management company Fable Security. “A modern risk program should have ensured he understood the modern [attack] surface of social engineering that attackers are using today.” Binance did not respond to CSO’s questions on whether it had policies in place that explicitly prohibited the developer’s actions on work computers and whether its employee training covered the fake recruitment social engineering tactic commonly used by North Korean hackers. An overprivileged AI tool enables lateral movement Once the attackers had malware running on the engineer’s computer, they were able to use an internal AI tool present on it to pivot to additional machines belonging to two other engineers from the wallet infrastructure team. Binance did not clarify the purpose of this tool in its report or to CSO, but the fact that it could be used by one compromised user to access different computers suggests its privileges were too broad or that it lacked proper access controls . This is hinted at by the company in its list of remediation steps, which included: “Rebuilt the affected internal AI tool and access controls.” On one of the additional engineering computers, the attackers found a token with permissions to deploy new containers on the company’s infrastructure. Nine days later they used this token on a different compromised engineering computer to deploy a container with a malicious script that interacted with the wallet signing service and initiated withdrawals. This series of events raises additional questions about credential hygiene and access controls because Binance’s report doesn’t describe any additional checks. Why was the token long-lived and not ephemeral for a single operation? Did deployment of containers to production involve additional validation or approval steps? Is there any authentication between the deployed container and the signing service, or was being on the same trusted network enough? Binance did not respond to CSO’s questions about any of these points. “An internal AI tool that can reach engineers’ systems holds the same kind of access as a privileged employee, and most organizations don’t govern it that way,” says Justin Beals, CEO of Strike Graph. “Expect more groups to copy this playbook against anyone holding signing keys, deployment tokens, or production access. Security leaders should treat engineers with production access, and the AI tools those engineers use, as privileged identities. That means restricting what gets installed on work machines, expiring deployment tokens quickly, and logging and reviewing what internal AI tools actually do.” Shlomi Salem, co-founder of Neo, a startup focused on AI agent security, predicted the AI attack vector days before Binance released its findings. “I wouldn’t be surprised if investigators find a poisoned package, a misused agent, or both at the start of this chain,” he said on Oct. 30 after the breach was announced. The takeaway for organizations is that internal AI tools are now part of the attack surface and need to be tested accordingly, Bri Frost, director of product management at Cloud Range, tells CSO. “When an AI tool can reach other systems on an employee’s behalf, an attacker who controls that employee’s machine may inherit everything the tool can do,” she says. “That changes the question security teams need to answer. It’s not only whether the model gives good answers, but what it will do, and for whom, when a request comes from a compromised session.”

The improper monitoring and access scoping of an internal AI tool played a major role in helping the hackers, and should serve as a warning for enterprise CISOs to take AI governance seriously. title: OpenAI built an AI pipeline to find, exploit and patch Linux flaws
raw_text: OpenAI has developed an autonomous AI pipeline that can identify software vulnerabilities, develop working exploits to validate their impact and generate patches for human review. In an October experiment targeting the Linux kernel, the pipeline created exploits for 948 distinct local privilege-escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities at a total API cost of $1.2 million, the company said in a November 4 research report, “ A thousand fewer paths to root .” The system automates vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploit development and patch generation. Human researchers still review the root-cause analysis, proof-of-concept exploits and proposed fixes before findings are reported to maintainers, OpenAI said. The research builds on OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative . Announcing the project in June as part of its Daybreak cybersecurity effort, the company said GPT-5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 LPE exploits. The latest experiment extends that work into a pipeline covering discovery, exploitation and patch generation, the report added. AI changes the economics of vulnerability research The October campaign cost $1,213,430 in API credits, averaging $1,279 per distinct LPE exploit created, OpenAI said. OpenAI compared its research expenditure with historical Linux kernel vulnerability bounty rewards offered by the Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN hacking competitions, which have paid $20,000 to $70,000 for LPE exploits. Based on those numbers, OpenAI estimated the value of the 948 exploits it created at between $18.9 million and $66.3 million, or 16 to 55 times the pipeline’s cost. The comparison does not represent actual bounty payouts or establish that every finding would qualify for those rewards. The latest campaign identified five times more unique LPE vulnerabilities than an earlier experiment using GPT-5.6 Sol, despite three months of additional hardening of the Linux kernel between the scans, OpenAI said. It also reported that its agents used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques based on its analysis of a sample of 166 of the exploits. The pipeline generated candidate patches for the validated vulnerabilities and used iterative testing and variant analysis to improve them, OpenAI said, adding that initial patches sometimes introduced unnecessary code changes or performance trade-offs, or failed to address related vulnerability variants. Humans still needed in the loop While the campaign was going on and before OpenAI could report its results to Linux kernel maintainers, 61 of the vulnerabilities it discovered had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and another 299 were being publicly discussed. OpenAI said it had submitted hundreds of vulnerability reports and patches to maintainers. The report did not provide a complete remediation breakdown for all 948 findings. The need to validate AI-generated exploits is another brake on reporting. During an early experiment, OpenAI found that 20 of 200 purportedly successful exploits had obtained root privileges by exploiting a different zero-day vulnerability than the one assigned for analysis. The company subsequently introduced additional checks to ensure its AI performed the assigned work. Enterprises evaluating autonomous security tools should demand reproducible exploits, accurate root-cause identification and independent validation, said Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO at Security Brigade. “Achieving a result and correctly explaining how you achieved it are two different things,” he said. Enterprise patching remains a challenge While OpenAI focused on the number of exploits it had found, that’s not the biggest threat, said Sakshi Grover, research director at IDC. “The risk is less the 948 than the length of the window between discovery and fixes reaching production,” she said. An upstream patch does not necessarily mean that the fix has reached the Linux distribution kernel running in an enterprise environment, Grover said. She recommended prioritizing multi-tenant hosts, CI/CD runners, shared bastions, container platforms and developer fleets, and seeking backport timelines from Linux distributors. Thomas Di Giacomo, chief technology and product officer at SUSE, said the company is using similar AI tools to discover and remediate vulnerabilities while working with upstream communities on disclosure and patching. “AI accelerating code analysis and bug hunting represents a fundamental shift in the threat landscape,” Di Giacomo said. He said SUSE’s enterprise Linux security approach combines multiple layers of protection with hardened runtimes for customer applications to mitigate privilege-escalation and container-escape risks. OpenAI added that it plans to extend the research to other critical software projects through Patch the Planet, working with maintainers and security partners on vulnerability discovery, validation and automated patching.

title: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber ups the ante on vulnerability discovery
raw_text: OpenAI is introducing GPT-6 Cyber, a restricted access model that the company calls its most capable and aligned cybersecurity model yet, “built to help security researchers identify and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, assess their impact, and harden potential patches before they’re released.” OpenAI researchers said they used GPT-6 Cyber to find 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox and develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including 588 previously unknown vulnerabilities. Mozilla has begun releasing fixes, and Linux findings are being reported with candidate patches for maintainer review. In a sample of 166 exploits, OpenAI’s researchers identified 10 exploitation techniques that the company says appeared novel, meaning external kernel exploitation experts reportedly had not seen them before, and that could enable someone with local access to obtain root privileges. Highlighting what it called stronger alignment and safeguards, OpenAI said that GPT-6 Cyber “was trained to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.” In its ExploitGym Honeypot evaluation, the model went beyond the intended scope in only 0.07% of cases, compared with 5.51% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. More bugs, new exploitation paths Chris Hughes, VP of security strategy at Noma Security, believes the Firefox findings suggest a deeper reservoir of vulnerabilities in mature software than defenders may have anticipated. “Mozilla says GPT-6 Cyber surfaced high-severity Firefox bugs after multiple generations of frontier models had already hardened that code,” Hughes told CSO. “If that holds up, the long tail of vulnerabilities in mature software is deeper than most of us assumed, which is the same ‘vulnpocalypse’ pressure many have been discussing this year.” Beyond that, the 10 novel techniques might point to how AI models could not only unearth more vulnerabilities but also create new exploitation paths, according to Rob T. Lee, the new chief AI officer at industrial cybersecurity company Dragos, which recently partnered with OpenAI. “That could mean a few things, but that’s interesting to me as it could reveal models can create new exploitation paths,” Lee told CSO. “Adding new TTPs and exploitation paths will make detection more complex.” (Rob T. Lee just joined Dragos, which is run by company founder and CEO Rob M. Lee.) The promise of security at agent speed During a press call to discuss GPT-6 Cyber, OpenAI’s representatives argued that models can help validate exploitability, investigate alternative attack paths, harden patches, and assist with patch deployment. They described the goal as security operating at “agent speed.” OpenAI researcher Eric Wallace said the goal was to “validate the potential exploitability of vulnerabilities at scale” and prioritize the most consequential flaws. He also emphasized testing fixes against alternative routes of exploitation, noting that “one vulnerability might not be the only attack path.” During the call, OpenAI cybersecurity research lead Clint Gibler touched on advance coordination the company engaged in regarding PHP vulnerabilities with researchers, maintainers, and security vendors. “We wanted to get ahead of that public patch and release, so that as many users and companies could be protected even before the patch was available,” he said. OpenAI worked with Cloudflare “to ensure that they could deploy WAF [web application firewall] rules, which would proactively protect as many websites as possible even before the bug was announced.” Finding flaws is easier to measure than fixing them OpenAI, however, provided no measurements showing how much its models accelerate enterprise patch deployment or reduce exposure. Noma Security’s Hughes argued that defensive applications need more rigorous evaluation, telling CSO, “Detection engineering, incident response, hardening, and prioritization are harder to score because success depends on each organization’s environment, tooling, and risk tolerance.” He believes that sharing defender benchmarks would direct progress toward “the work that closes the remediation gap, not only toward finding more bugs.” Hughes added: “The OpenAI Patch the Planet dashboard currently shows a less than 25% remediation rate thus far, and given the improved finding capability, this is likely to exacerbate that further, meaning more things found but unfixed and likely to be found by malicious actors with similar capabilities or effective harness engineering on sub-tier models. This highlights even further risk for organizations facing the rise of industrialized discovery via AI.” Stronger safeguards, restricted access OpenAI classifies GPT-6 Cyber as “Critical” in cybersecurity under its own Preparedness Framework. “Going out of scope in 0.07% of cases versus 5.51% for the prior model is a real improvement,” Hughes noted. “At the scale these models operate, though, even a small fraction means actions against systems nobody authorized.” OpenAI said that GPT-6 Cyber will initially be available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers, the more permissive of two vetted access tiers in Daybreak, OpenAI’s trusted-access cyber program . (Daybreak Blue is the tier OpenAI recommends for most defenders.) OpenAI said it will progressively expand GPT-6 Cyber access to all Daybreak Red customers over the coming weeks, and is making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to that customer set as well. OpenAI said in briefing materials prior to the press call, “We are working to responsibly expand access to frontier cyber capabilities to many more organizations and members of the security community. To start, we’re broadening access to an alpha of Daybreak Blue for Astra ,” which is OpenAI’s GPT-6 general-purpose frontier model.

title: Debian, Ubuntu patch APT flaw that could hand attackers root
raw_text: Linux administrators’ trust in package managers is being tested by a newly disclosed vulnerability in APT, the package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and their derivatives, that could allow attackers to install unverified software with root privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-109518 , the vulnerability could let an attacker positioned to manipulate HTTP traffic between an APT client and an archive server install an attacker-controlled package without verification. Debian disclosed the flaw on November 4, crediting security researcher Max Justicz. Ubuntu subsequently rated it High, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.7. “I used an AI for two hours and found a zero-day that would let a nation-state hack any server running stock Ubuntu,” Justicz said in an X post . Successful exploitation could allow arbitrary code execution with root privileges on a vulnerable machine. Both distributions have issued fixes. Redirects and retries turn hardlinks into an attack surface The problem lies in APT’s handling of HTTP redirects and resumed downloads. “APT can merge two different package downloads after an HTTP redirect gives them the same URI,” Debian’s advisory said. “Improper file handling when resuming an HTTP download allows a man-in-the-middle ( MitM ) attacker to replace a package after verification, resulting in the execution of arbitrary code as root.” APT developers provide a more detailed explanation: an attacker can exploit redirects and transient HTTP server errors that trigger download retries, causing APT to override existing hard links with a chosen payload. Because Debian packages are installed with root privileges, successfully substituting a package can lead to arbitrary code execution as root. Ubuntu described the required attack position as an on-path attacker able to manipulate traffic between the package client and the archive server. A malicious mirror or proxy could provide that position, but the attack requires specific download conditions. Retry settings decide who is exposed The vulnerability depends on APT’s Acquire::Retries setting being non-zero. APT developers say this has been the default since version 2.3.2, although scripts may have enabled retries on older installations. Ubuntu specifies that the default retry value of three applies from Debian 12 (Bookworm) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) onward. Older releases are not exposed by default, but may still be vulnerable if retries have been enabled. Debian 13 (Trixie) is patched in APT 3.0.4, while Debian 12 (Bookworm) received the fix in version 2.6.2. Ubuntu has also released patched packages for supported releases, including 22.04 LTS, 24.04.LTS, and 26.04 LTS. Ubuntu 26.10 was also affected, with its fix being published when Ubuntu’s November 4 advisory appeared. The fix addresses the underlying file-handling issue. In a commit authored on October 12, APT developer Julian Andres Klode changed the download code to open destination files exclusively, unlinking existing files before copying over any partially downloaded content. The change prevents downloads from writing through existing hard links, which could otherwise redirect writes to unintended files. Ubuntu recommends updating APT and temporarily disabling retries during remediation. It also advises using HTTPS for package downloads, which protects against traffic manipulation in this attack scenario. For enterprise security teams, the priority is to identify vulnerable installations, check retry configurations, and ensure patched packages reach production systems and the Linux images used to provision them.

title: Zyxel patches a zero-day hiding behind an old fix
raw_text: Zyxel has patched a zero-day vulnerability that attackers exploited to compromise 996 GS1900 network switches across 48 countries, exposing device configurations, network information and hashed root credentials. The attack began around August 17, according to cybersecurity firm GreyNoise, but researchers initially blamed a different vulnerability that Zyxel had already addressed. The newly identified flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-107441 , is a CVSS 8.8 out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the switches’ web management interface. It allows unauthenticated attackers with network access to execute operating system commands through specially crafted HTTP requests. The flaw affects ten GS1900 models, including GS1900-8, GS1900-24, and GS1900-48. Zyxel listed firmware versions ending in .2C0 and earlier as vulnerable, with model-specific fixes in versions ending in .3C0. Zyxel released a fix for CVE-2026-7273 in June, addressing a separate buffer overflow in the same switch series. GreyNoise initially attributed the attacks to that vulnerability, prompting CISA to add it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog in September. However, security researchers at Binary discovered an exploit targeting a previously unknown flaw that remained effective even on switches running the June updates. The researchers reported the vulnerability to Zyxel on September 29. The attackers used a script to collect device configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Such data can give intruders a useful map of an organization’s network and potentially help them move deeper into its infrastructure. Zyxel released firmware updates on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3. Administrators should update affected GS1900 switches, including those already running June security fixes.

title: Building incident playbooks for machine identity breaches
raw_text: Pull up your SOC’s compromised account playbook and read through the first 15 minutes. Most SOCs begin their response by calling or messaging the user via Teams to ask whether the 2:00 am sign-in from an unfamiliar country was indeed them. Their subsequent actions depend upon what the user responds with. Try that with a service account, and you’ll be waiting a long time. The same goes for an API key buried in a build pipeline, or an OAuth token somebody granted to a SaaS integration back in 2022 and hasn’t thought about since. Once one of those is stolen, your analysts are running a script that was written with people in mind, and the cracks tend to show well before the first shift handover. There are also far more of them than most boards realise. CyberArk’s research puts machine identities at roughly 82 for every human identity . Very few sit behind MFA, and a fair number hold far more access than the job they were built for. I’d add a problem that gets less airtime, which is that their traffic lives in the background noise your monitoring was tuned to filter out. Where the human playbook stalls Ownership is usually the first thing to slow you down. When a person’s account is compromised, HR can tell you who they are and who their manager is before you’ve finished your coffee. A service account pulling data it shouldn’t comes with no such shortcut, so the analyst burns the first hour working out which team built it. More often than anyone likes to admit, that trail ends at a contractor who left the business a year earlier. Say you do find an owner; containment still isn’t the clean step it is for a person. Lock a user out and one employee loses an afternoon. Pull a credential that a payments integration depends on, though, and you might take a customer-facing service down, which no analyst wants on their name at 11 p.m. without sign-off. So, they go hunting for somebody senior enough to approve the outage while the attacker carries on. Detection is the part people underestimate. An attacker with a valid token makes authenticated calls to the same endpoints the integration hits every day, and a patient one will even keep to its usual hours. Your impossible-travel rules were built around people moving between cities, so they have nothing to compare against here. Figure 1: One alert split into two paths. Ashish Mishra What recent breaches show Cloudflare’s write-up of its Thanksgiving 2023 security incident is worth a quarter of an hour of any CISO’s time. The attackers came in with one access token and three service account credentials lifted during the earlier Okta support breach. Cloudflare had rotated thousands of credentials after Okta, yet missed those four because the team believed, wrongly, that nothing was using them. The alert that finally fired came more than a week after the attackers first logged in, when they added one of those service accounts to an administrator group. Microsoft’s case turned on a test application nobody had cleaned up. Its guidance for responders on the Midnight Blizzard attack describes a password spray against a legacy test tenant account with no MFA. Inside that tenant sat an old test OAuth app that still held elevated access to the corporate environment, and the attackers used it to get into corporate email accounts. Drift is the case I’d put in front of a board. In August 2025, attackers got hold of the OAuth tokens that Salesloft’s Drift chatbot used to talk to Salesforce, and for roughly ten days they pulled records out of one customer’s Salesforce instance after another. Google’s threat intelligence team, which tracked the campaign closely , concluded the attackers were mostly after credentials. Once the data was out, they went digging through it for AWS access keys and passwords, anything that might get them into the next company along. I don’t think any of the three needed a clever attacker at the front door. In each case, a credential was issued for a piece of work and then left alone long after the work had finished. Getting the groundwork in first It is a relatively simple task to create a playbook. However, a playbook relies upon an inventory. In many organizations, this inventory consists of a service account list generated from Active Directory where half of the description fields have been left blank. Each time you identify a high-privilege non-human identity, document the team responsible for that identity, and provide a brief explanation (one or two sentences) describing what will fail should you remove that identity. Many people do not include the explanation as to why something would fail if removed, since obtaining this information requires contacting the application team for clarification; this contact would otherwise be initiated by your analyst at 3:00 AM while the attacker remains active within your network. Next, sort those identities by blast radius. I wouldn’t put a read-only reporting token on the same response path as a cloud admin service principal, and I doubt your auditors would either. For the top tier, settle in advance who’s allowed to authorise an immediate revoke even if it knocks something over, and put that role in the playbook by name. Executives must own that call. If you leave it with whoever’s on shift, you’ll get a polite wait for permission while the token stays live. For SOCI-regulated entities, there’s an extra edge to this, because the 12-hour window for reporting a significant cyber incident to ASD can be running while that conversation drags on. Triage that fits a machine No one can provide a response to “was this you?”, thus, replace it with questions that can be answered by the log files. A rapid means of verification is location: where do the credentials usually sign in from, and where are they signing in from at present? Logging is readily available via Cloud Audit Logs and Workload Identity Platforms, if someone turned the logging on. Permissions take longer but tell you more. Line up what the identity holds against what it has used over the last few months, because attackers tend to go straight for high-risk scopes that have been sitting idle. I’d give persistence the same attention. With a privileged service principal in hand, an attacker will often mint new secrets or register an app of their own, and none of that goes away when you revoke the original credential. Containment without breaking the business The “trigger” for rotation and revocation should be written separately in the playbook. Rotation would be appropriate when you are reasonably confident that the attacker has not escalated and the organization cannot afford to lose the integration. Revocation is the obvious choice if you find evidence of an ongoing attack; this will be clear enough so there will be no debate at midnight. Pre-staging your replacement credentials will make revocations tolerable. When the team that owns the application has previously tested how to generate a new credential and then store it in their secret management system, revoking old credentials can cost you about ten minutes of downtime instead of being a full-day disruption. Ask the team to practice generating and storing new credentials during a low-traffic week. Do not find out mid-incident that the runbook references a vault location that was renamed last year. Scoping and recovery To understand the full scope of an incident, look at the entire lifespan of the machine credential, not just the period after the alert was generated. Because machines may be able to go undetected as being compromised for many months prior to discovery, the first unusual activity reported will most likely not be the first unusual activity performed. Also, keep in mind that “drift” is a great way to remember to see what information the identity has access to, and if anyone has placed credentials into that identity. If so, each addition of a secret will require you to add a new rotation to your list. Recovery is when you fix what caused the problem in the first place. For example, if a static secret was compromised, determine if that workload can use short-lived tokens using Workload Identity Federation; or perhaps a short-lived token can be generated on demand (Just-In-Time) and will expire automatically. Recovery is a tedious, non-sexy task, and most of the time it requires financial support from an entity outside of the Security Operations Center (SOC). Before finalizing the playbook, conduct a tabletop simulation with the application owners in attendance along with the Security Operations Center (SOC). Select your highest-privilege integration and simulate a stolen-token event (from first alert through recovery). During the simulation, when a decision needs to be made regarding who approves revoking the token, and revoking the token will disrupt production, observe how much time it takes for the team to identify who should make this approval.
summary: Pull up your SOC’s compromised account playbook and read through the first 15 minutes. Most SOCs begin their response by calling or messaging the user via Teams to ask whether the 2:00 am sign-in from an unfamiliar country was indeed them. Their subsequent actions depend upon what the user responds with. Try that with a service account, and you’ll be waiting a long time.

title: The Sandbox Fights Back: Joe Security Launches Adaptive Detonation
raw_text: AI agents help Joe Sandbox uncover malicious behavior concealed by evasion techniques and unmet execution conditions. Joe Security ‘s Adaptive Detonation brings active intervention to malware analysis, helping security teams investigate threats that may conceal their behavior during an initial sandbox run. Adaptive Detonation uses AI agents to examine execution results, identify obstacles preventing a sample from revealing relevant behavior, and select targeted interventions. These can include patching a blocking check, creating required files or settings, adjusting the execution environment, or supplying missing command-line arguments. Joe Sandbox then analyzes the sample again under the modified conditions to verify whether the intervention reveals additional activity. The approach addresses obstacles including keyboard restrictions, timing checks, firmware-based rejection, date requirements, and missing dependencies. By connecting observed evidence with targeted action and verification, Adaptive Detonation helps analysts investigate why a sample remains inactive and uncover behavior that might otherwise stay hidden. For security teams, this means deeper visibility into evasive threats and more evidence to support investigations. Adaptive Detonation is available as part of Joe Sandbox AI, a plugin for Joe Sandbox Cloud. Security teams can test Joe Sandbox by signing in or registering for Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic , the free community version. title: Attackers turned OpsShield’s trusted update channel into a supply-chain attack
raw_text: The kinks in the software supply chain are once again being exposed, with attackers now targeting OpsShield’s update process. This week, threat actors used compromised credentials to push malicious updates out to cPGuard customers. They then accessed data stored on the vendor’s servers and in its billing portal accounts, and made copies of at least three of OpsShield’s cloud servers. The company said in an advisory that it has “shut the attacker out of every system we know they reached, and … are rebuilding the ones we cannot fully trust.” It has also released updates and urges customers to update to the latest version of cPGuard, change passwords, and generate new SSH keys. Ultimately, the breadth of this unsanctioned access underscores the continued fragility of the software supply chain, as well as the vulnerability of security tools themselves. “The real danger here is that attackers were able to turn a trusted security update mechanism into a vector to break into servers,” said Erik Avakian , a technical counselor at Infotech. “The software that’s supposed to protect those servers became the source that compromised them.” The anatomy of the attack OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software. Its cPGuard product is a security suite, malware scanner, and firewall designed for Linux web hosting servers. The company disclosed that, between November 1 and 2, attackers were able to gain unauthorized access to the OpsShield update distribution infrastructure, and, for about 70 minutes, pushed out a malicious update. The threat actors began by probing OpsShield’s billing portal, registering a customer account under a false identity, and ordering a free cPGuard trial. They then sent crafted requests that allowed them to gain the ability to run commands on the server to collect data. They used stolen access keys to publish fake updates that ran as root (the highest level of admin privilege), and to copy sensitive files and make copies of three OpsShield cloud servers. About 2,950 customer servers ran the fake update, exposing password hashes, root SSH keys, MySQL root passwords, and shell history, OpsShield reported. Attackers also accessed about 7,900 billing portal accounts containing customer names, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords. OpsShield says it is still reviewing the exact request that provided access, and has patched two possible entry points and verified related vendor components “line by line.” It closed the attacker’s account, revoked the stolen update-storage key as well as “every cloud API token and access key on our account.” The company also removed the attacker’s secure shell (SSH); deleted the clones of its servers created by the attacker plus any snapshots; turned on stronger login protection and replaced every SSH key and password; reset all billing portal login sessions and rotated all keys; and began rebuilding its billing, licensing, and internal management servers with tighter PHP and firewall settings. The company has also published clean updates: v5.88.26, which removes the hidden root shell; plus a follow-up which removes the scheduled task left by the attacker. Further, it began re-issuing all cPGuard license private and public keys so that the copies the attacker gained access to stopped working. The company advised admins to: Update cPGuard to the latest version, then confirm that /etc/cron.d/i93677 , /var/tmp/.i93677/ and /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh are gone; delete them if not; Change root passwords and every local user password on the server; Generate new root SSH keys and remove old ones from every server that trusted them; until the keys are changed, treat the servers as compromised; Change MySQL root passwords and any database passwords and rotate any password, API key, or token existing in root shell histories; Reset the OpsShield billing portal passwords and turn on two-factor authentication. Finally, it said, “if we told you the attacker logged in to your server by hand, rebuild it from a clean backup taken before 1 November.” OpsShield being transparent, but the impacts are still real “Frankly, few vendors write a breach disclosure this candid,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “OpsShield deserves a lot of credit for that.” However, he pointed out, the worst kind of breach is the one a security tool delivers. Update channels are left unlocked on purpose, and security tools run as root because they have to see everything, “so the fake update ran as root too.” For a hosting provider, one server can hold hundreds of customer websites and databases. A MySQL root password opens all of them, and a root SSH key grants access to every other server that trusts it. Shell history also often contains typed passwords and tokens. The downstream customer may be hit hardest while knowing the least, Dickson pointed out, as most website owners have no idea which security agent their hosting provider runs. Every server that updates itself trusts the vendor’s pipeline. OpsShield describes itself as a small team selling to smaller hosts at a low price, which is the uncomfortable truth of the supply chain, Dickson said. “Your exposure is set by the smallest vendor holding root on your servers, not the largest.” Avakian agreed that this serves as a reminder that an enterprise’s software supply chain is only as secure as the systems, identities, and processes behind it. “You can do everything you can to secure your own infrastructure and still get compromised through a third-party supplier you trust.” What’s particularly concerning here is that the attackers didn’t have to go after thousands of customers one by one; they only had to compromise a single distribution mechanism to turn the vendor’s own trusted infrastructure against its customers, he noted. Third parties extend risk, which is a fact that organizations still underestimate, he said. “Enterprises need to pay much more attention to third-party and supply chain risk management.” Zero-trust a must-have Avakian also pointed out that the impact on downstream customers could go well beyond initial compromise, as stolen credentials can be used to carry out further attacks. Enterprises should take a zero-trust approach that includes their software suppliers and the updates they rely on. “Just because an update comes from a trusted source doesn’t mean you can assume it’s safe,” he said. Enterprises should take a closer look at vendor risk, protect privileged credentials, and examine software integrity. Also, continuously monitor for unexpected behavior after an update and be ready to isolate systems quickly if and when something goes wrong. “You have to plan for the possibility that even a trusted supplier can be compromised,” he emphasized. “And you need to practice those types of scenarios as part of a regular table-top exercise program.” Dickson advised starting with an inventory, and knowing every vendor agent running with root or administrator privilege, as each one is an update channel. Customers should ask vendors where update publishing keys live and what separates them from customer-facing systems, watch outbound traffic from servers, keep secrets out of shell history, and treat SSH keys as credentials with an expiration date. Downstream customers should ask their host directly whether it runs cPGuard, then change their own passwords. “The most dangerous software on your server may be the software you trust to update itself,” he said. “Choose those vendors as if they hold root, because they do.” This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld .

This week, threat actors used compromised credentials to push malicious updates out to cPGuard customers. They then accessed data stored on the vendor’s servers and in its billing portal accounts, and made copies of at least three of OpsShield’s cloud servers. The company said in an advisory that it has “shut the attacker out of every system we know they reached, and … are rebuilding the ones we cannot fully trust.” It has also released updates and urges customers to update to the latest version of cPGuard, change passwords, and generate new SSH keys.

title: Fake software installers are turning your PCs into profit centers for hackers
raw_text: Users looking for cracked commercial software, free games, plugins, and unofficial utilities could be signing up for more than a free download. Microsoft has observed an evolving campaign that uses trojanized installers to turn the downloading Windows devices into money-making machines, consuming their computing resources and internet bandwidth without informed consent. The campaign uses fake download pages and Inno Setup-style installers to deliver multiple software packages during a single installation session, Microsoft said in a blog post. The campaign was found distributing three monetization components, some of which may have legitimate uses when installed knowingly. “Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms,” the company said , adding that its Defender XDR detects and blocks several payloads and behaviors related to the campaign. Fake installers used for real money The campaign begins with users downloading installers advertised as cracked software , games, activators, plugins, or unofficial utilities. Microsoft observed lures posing as products like Navicat Premium and FabFilter audio plugins, alongside gaming and utility downloads. The installers use an Inno Setup-style wrapper to stage temporary executables under Windows’ temporary directories. Numbered payloads subsequently execute and coordinate the delivery of additional software. Microsoft said the campaign features an offer-based delivery mechanism. The installer communicates with rotating infrastructure using HTTP callbacks containing parameters such as “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution”. These requests allow the campaign to track individual software offers, allowing multiple payloads to succeed or fail independently within the same installation session. The first monetization branch is WorldProxyPool, which installs proxyware to route third-party internet traffic through the victim’s device. It also creates SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updates. Another branch installs CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC), alongside components such as VirtualBox, to facilitate distributed computing. A third installs utility-style software associated with Advanced Windows Manager and Windows Manager. These applications may participate in advertising, software distribution, or affiliate-driven monetization. Microsoft urges defenders to scrutinize unofficial software Microsoft recommends preventing downloads from untrusted sources, particularly cracked software, key generators , unofficial game installers, and activation tools. Organizations using Microsoft Defender Antivirus should enable cloud-delivered protection, maintain tamper protection, and configure reputation-based protection to block untrusted applications and downloads, the company said. It also recommends evaluating Attack Surface Reduction ( ASR ) rules that restrict executable files based on prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria. For detection and investigation, organizations were advised to check execution from Inno temporary directories, especially when files such as “eld*.exe, set_*.exe”, “FirstFast[1].exe”, or “SecondRunner[1].exe” appear. Microsoft also recommends correlating outbound requests containing “d=inno” and “r=offer_execution” or “r=offer_execution_fail” with process activity, scheduled-task creation, and software installations. Unexpected WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, or VirtualBox installations warrant investigation, it said. Defender XDR customers can use Microsoft’s published advanced hunting queries to identify related activity, while a list of indicators of compromise (IOCs) was also shared to help defenders outside the Microsoft ecosystem.

title: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch to shut down rogue agents
raw_text: With a notable rise in autonomous AI agents veering off-script inside corporate networks, CrowdStrike has launched an enterprise AI Kill Switch, giving security teams control to cut off and disable models when they go rogue . Integrated into its Falcon Guardian platform, this AI Kill Switch will provide security teams with the human control to terminate the agent at its root, where it runs, block it from launching again, and even cut off its enterprise network access. The launch comes as enterprises increasingly deploy autonomous AI agents that can access sensitive data and execute tasks with limited human oversight. “These agents can access sensitive data, execute commands and interact with business applications independently, meaning enterprises may become aware of harmful incidents only after they occur. Existing security tools protect endpoints, networks and identities but may not fully understand an agent’s instructions, reasoning, tool calls and subsequent actions,” said Soumen Mandal, principal analyst at Counterpoint Research. Inside CrowdStrike’s AI kill switch The AI Kill Switch has been built on Falcon Guardian, which has the capability to discover the AI agents running in the enterprise. It uses the Falcon sensor to track what an agent is instructed to do, what it communicates, and what it executes. First, the Falcon sensor can terminate the running agent at the gateway, ensuring the malicious or misbehaving agent does not keep running while teams investigate. CrowdStrike said endpoint termination is also planned and will be available soon. Next, using the Falcon Guardian policies, the kill switch will prevent the agent from launching again on the targeted host or group of hosts. Next, it will cut-off agent’s enterprise network access. The action can be initiated by an authorised administrator, with every action being recorded in an audit trail. “Solutions such as CrowdStrike’s AI Kill Switch give enterprises a way to intervene quickly when AI agents behave unexpectedly, are compromised, or are manipulated through malicious instructions or scripts. This provides an important safeguard, allowing organisations to contain potentially dangerous or unauthorised agent activity before it causes significant damage,” said Devroop Dhar, MD and co-founder at Primus Partners. However, a kill switch should be viewed as an emergency brake, not a rewind button, said Apeksha Kaushik, senior principal analyst at Gartner. She added that it may prevent additional actions, but it might not necessarily reverse all the data that has already been accessed, every system that has already been changed, all communications that have already been sent, or transactions that have already been initiated. Its effectiveness will also depend on how quickly abnormal behavior is detected, which environments are covered, and whether the agent or security infrastructure has been compromised. An emergency brake, not a cure for AI risk An AI Kill Switch looks promising from the details provided, but its actual effectiveness will come in after it is used extensively in live systems, warn analysts. Also, it may be a good starting point, but it cannot be viewed as a standalone solution to enterprise AI security. “CISOs would need a more integrated approach that brings together AI discovery tools to identify unauthorised agents, runtime monitoring to track agent behaviour, robust identity and access management, and incident response and recovery mechanisms,” added Dhar. He noted that equally important is the need for stringent AI security testing and clearly defined policies governing what agents can access and execute. There should be no ambiguity around permissions, access controls or the boundaries within which these agents are allowed to operate. The objective should be to ensure that security controls are built into the entire AI agent lifecycle rather than relying on a kill switch to intervene after something goes wrong. Dhar added that enterprise AI agents often have access to sensitive systems, databases, applications, credentials, and APIs. A compromised or misdirected agent could therefore become a point of vulnerability. The challenge is compounded by the fact that such activity may go undetected for some time, making it difficult for organisations to identify and contain the threat.

title: CrowdStrike to acquire Fiddler, Dreadnode to extend AI security across agent lifecycle
raw_text: CrowdStrike plans to acquire AI security companies Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in separate deals that will extend its Falcon platform into automated testing of AI systems and monitoring of AI agent behaviour, as enterprises look to address security risks arising from increasingly autonomous applications. CrowdStrike made the announcements at Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona, saying the acquisitions will add capabilities to test AI models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment and monitor their decisions and actions in production. The company plans to integrate Dreadnode’s automated testing technology and Fiddler’s agent observability capabilities into Falcon, with both offerings scheduled for general availability in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027. Dreadnode will bring automated security testing to identify vulnerabilities in AI models, applications and agents before deployment. Fiddler, meanwhile, will add AI agent observability and explainability, allowing enterprises to monitor agent behaviour, trace decisions and understand why agents take particular actions, CrowdStrike said in two separate statements. CrowdStrike said the Dreadnode team will join its Cyber Superintelligence Lab, but did not specify how the Fiddler team would be integrated into the company. CrowdStrike adds AI testing and observability “With this acquisition, Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform into the layer where enterprises build and test AI, delivering Automated AI Security Testing capabilities,” CrowdStrike said in its announcement. It further added that Dreadnode’s technology will allow security teams to test AI models, applications, agent reasoning loops and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers against more than 100 AI attack strategies. These include jailbreaks, prompt injection, multi-turn attacks, and attacks targeting AI agents. The technology will also let teams describe tests in natural language, rank findings by severity, and map vulnerabilities to frameworks including OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, OWASP Agentic Security, MITRE ATLAS, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. CrowdStrike said findings will feed into Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations. Fiddler, the second acquisition, will bring agent observability and explainability capabilities to Falcon. CrowdStrike said the technology is intended to address risks that can arise even when agents have not been compromised. “An agent can hold valid credentials and approved tools and still make unsupported decisions, ignore instructions, or claim work it never completed. They don’t have to be compromised to create risk,” the company said in a statement. CrowdStrike plans to offer Fiddler’s technology through Falcon Observe. The product will evaluate agent accuracy, task completion, and policy compliance before deployment, and trace decisions, reasoning paths, and tool calls once agents are in production, the company said. The company further added that Falcon Observe will also detect behavioural drift, hallucinations and unintended actions, while maintaining records of agent activity for compliance and audit purposes. The offering is expected to support OpenTelemetry and frameworks including LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Strands and Google ADK, it added. Governance remains a shared responsibility The addition of observability and automated testing to a security platform could help enterprises correlate agent behaviour with identity, runtime activity and security events, said Apeksha Kaushik, senior principal analyst at Gartner. However, Kaushik said the acquisitions would not make security teams the sole owners of AI agent governance. Platform and observability teams would continue to be responsible for reliability, performance and operational telemetry, while application security and AI teams would retain responsibility for secure development and testing. “Business, data and compliance leaders also retain accountability for use cases, data and regulatory obligations,” Kaushik said. She said CIOs should establish a governance model that defines responsibilities across engineering, security, risk, and business teams. CISOs, meanwhile, should ensure security teams have the authority to set minimum controls, monitor agent behaviour and intervene when activity creates unacceptable risk. Integration and roadmap questions CrowdStrike expects both transactions to close during its fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, and has scheduled both offerings for general availability in the same quarter. Kaushik cautioned enterprises against treating the announced timelines as confirmation of final product capabilities or integration plans. “Enterprises should distinguish between announced plans and demonstrated product capability, with closing timeline and conditions possibly being different, especially with the pace of change of the threat landscape and evolution of AI,” she added. She advised customers to seek clarity on pricing, packaging, migration terms, service continuity, support commitments, deployment models, data handling, telemetry retention and API access. “Once the Existing and prospective customers have further details, they should set up their roadmap changes, support commitments, service continuity, contract and pricing, data portability, open integrations, and access to historical data changes,” she pointed out. CrowdStrike did not disclose the financial terms of either acquisition.

title: Zurich uncovers £19m of fraud with Quantexa data analytics
raw_text:
Zurich UK has discovered £109.3m worth of fraud over the past year using data analytics technology from Quantexa.

The insurer has deployed the technology over the past year, exposing the work of criminal gangs involved in so-called crash-for-cash scams and other fraudulent schemes.

Scott Clayton, head of claims fraud at Zurich UK and chair of the Insurance Fraud Bureau (IFB), said: “Insurance fraud in the UK is becoming more sophisticated, more organised and increasingly technology-enabled. Criminal networks are constantly adapting their tactics, whether that’s staged accidents, ghost broking, fabricated claims or the use of AI-generated evidence.”

Ghost broking is a technique and practice whereby fraudsters pose as bona fide brokers to sell car insurance policies that are fake or invalid.

Clayton added: “The £109m of fraud we’ve uncovered this year shows both the scale of the threat and the importance of staying ahead of it. Connected data is transforming the fight against fraud, helping us expose hidden relationships, identify organised networks and protect honest customers from footing the bill for criminal activity. The combination of advanced analytics, specialist investigators and human judgement is proving a powerful defence against a rapidly evolving threat.

“We’re the first insurer in the UK to use technology that brings together information from Companies House, Equifax, industry intelligence and the Insurance Fraud Register to give us a much richer picture across every claim. That helps us identify crucial connections and information that might otherwise be difficult to spot.”

Quantexa and Zurich calculate the volume of fraud as equivalent to one claim every two hours.

They claim Zurich has uncovered a fraud network involving more than 90 UK claims, where drivers were deliberately targeted on roundabouts, with fraudsters exploiting blind spots and lane changes to cause collisions.

They said the fraudsters deliberately caused more than 100 accidents, creating claims worth over £1m.

Quantexa’s AI and advanced analytics software is said to have helped identify 860 fraudulent claims worth £17.9m, amounting to one in five of the fraud cases.

Zurich found 4,359 fraudulent claims across its casualty, motor and property categories. The number of fraudulent claims identified has risen by 22% from 3,562 in 2022 to 4,359 in the last year, it said.

The Quantexa technology has revealed links between suspicious claims and a common accident location, claimants using aliases to conceal previous activity, and organised fraud involving professional enablers such as rogue solicitors and accident management companies.

The platform is also said to have helped investigators identify people living in one part of the UK who were linked to suspected staged accidents hundreds of miles away. 

Vishal Marria, founder and CEO of Quantexa, said: “Fraud hides in the gaps between claims, which is why seeing the full context matters. By putting every claim in context, networks come into view, organised threats are stopped earlier, and genuine claims are dealt with more quickly.”

Ursula Jallow, executive director of the IFB, said: “Insurance fraud is becoming increasingly sophisticated and AI-driven, making it vital that we continue to invest in the systems, controls and partnerships needed to protect businesses and consumers.”

Zurich’s is not the only set of use cases for this technology. In 2023, the government’s Public Sector Fraud Authority (PSFA), which is part of the Cabinet Office and HM Treasury, signed a £4m deal with Quantexa to use artificial intelligence to find potential fraudsters.

And the advanced analytics supplier is one of a cohort popular with senior civil servants and politicians moving to the private sector. Computer Weekly counted four of 63 personnel moves between the public sector and 20 IT, cloud and AI suppliers from 2010 to 2026 as being to Quantexa.

title: Minority groups oppose ‘routine’ police facial recognition
raw_text:
Facial recognition technology (FRT) should not become a “routine or firsthand policing tool” in the UK, the Home Office-commissioned study into the views of minority groups has found.

Conducted as part of the government’s police biometrics consultation by Thinks Insight & Strategy, the study was run as “a small-scale deliberative dialogue” with 56 people, including those from racially minoritised communities, who were either cautious or opposed to the police use of facial recognition in the UK.

Published alongside the government’s formal response to its police biometrics consultation on 4 November 2026, the authors said “trust emerged as a central theme” of the study, which found that support for police use of facial recognition is “cautious and conditional”.

Rather than becoming a “routine” policing tool, participants instead “felt it should be used only where demonstrably necessary and proportionate, in clearly defined circumstances and subject to time limits and targeted deployment”.

They were also clear that UK law enforcement bodies will need to build trust in the communities they police before they roll out facial recognition more widely.

“While some participants believed that policing is largely undertaken by well-intentioned officers whose work is undermined by a minority of ‘bad apples’, others, particularly participants from Black African, Black Caribbean and Mixed Black backgrounds, described experiences of discriminatory treatment that had significantly impacted their confidence and trust in the police,” it said.

“This context is critical. Participants consistently assessed police and law enforcement use of facial recognition technology through the lens of whether they trust the police to use their powers fairly and proportionately.”

The study added that, within this context, safeguards and independent oversight were viewed by participants as necessary pre-conditions to building trust and increasing confidence in police use of these technologies.

As part of its wider police biometrics consultation response, the government welcomed the findings of the study, noting that it aligned with its “intention to provide greater public assurance and give police forces in England and Wales greater confidence to use facial recognition within a strong and well-defined legal framework”.

It added: “As part of the framework, the government intends to make public participation in oversight a statutory requirement for both police forces and the new independent oversight body.”

Specific concerns

Areas of particular concern for those involved in the study included the potential for inaccuracy or misidentification, the deliberate misuse of the technology by individual officers, bias and discrimination, disproportionate use, the stifling of freedom of expression, and scope creep.

Many of these areas interlock. For example, on the risks of bias and discrimination, participants cited the potential for the technology to disproportionately impact on racially minoritised communities through misidentification rates (linked to inaccuracy), over-deployment at cultural events attended by Black communities (which would stifle expression), and wider patterns of deployment that could contribute to the over-policing of Black communities.  

“Taken together, all of this information led to fear that police use of FRT could mean institutionalised entrenchment of existing bias against minoritised communities,” said the authors.

Participant concerns also overlapped when it came to the potential for disproportionate use and scope creep, with many feeling it would not be proportionate to use the technology for detecting individuals suspected of minor or petty crimes (which they felt was currently the case with how police forces use FRT), and expressing further concern over widespread deployment in public spaces without clear justification.

“Participants expressed an overarching concern that the ways in which facial recognition is used, and the purposes it is used for, could keep expanding,” it said.

“Given low levels of trust in police, participants feared that once normalised, safeguards around facial recognition technology use could gradually weaken. This raised concerns that these technologies could be used beyond their original, intended purposes as outlined in any new legal framework.”

To overcome the clear trust deficit, participants made a number of suggestions for how police facial recognition can be effectively regulated.

This included introducing strict rules to regulate access to government databases, stronger transparency requirements for police forces deploying the tech, and the creation of an independent oversight body, which many participants wanted to operate “without influence from the police or politicians”.

“They felt an independent body would ensure decisions are handled fairly, without bias in favour of police or policies,” the study’s authors wrote. “They were concerned that existing bodies have relationships with the police already, which could lead to decisions in favour of the police.”

In terms of what functions such an oversight body should have, participants suggested it could conduct pre-deployment approvals every time police want to use facial recognition, have strong powers to enforce against misuse, and conduct audits.

Participants were broadly in favour of public involvement in the oversight body, with some suggesting this involvement could be scheduled on a revolving basis, similar to how jury service operates.

Participants also emphasised the need for strict rules around necessity and proportionality.

“In exploring cases where someone had committed a less serious crime, participants felt the positives of catching that criminal did not outweigh the level of intrusion into privacy, or the risks of misidentification or over-surveillance,” the authors said, adding that participants also emphasised that FRT should be used only in cases where other means of solving the crime would not be effective.

“They did not consider FRT, and particularly Live FRT, to be a first line measure. Instead, it should only be used if a wanted criminal had not been caught through other means, and this criminal was a threat to public safety.”

In summarising the study, authors noted that while participants did not entirely reject the use of facial recognition by police, “they made clear that confidence in facial recognition will depend on its deployment having clear limits, fair use, strong accountability and independent oversight”.

While the government acknowledged the study – and in the process committed to statutory public participation in the oversight of police facial recognition – its wider consultation response lacks detail on what specific safeguards the government is considering, and how it will address wider concerns around bias and discrimination, proportionality and necessity (a key legal test for UK police), the protection of freedom of expression, and scope creep.

title: Home Office plans £881.6m AWS deal, at nearly three times spend rate
raw_text:
The Home Office plans to renew its Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud hosting at a potential cost of £881.6m over two years – nearly three times the annual rate of the £450m three-year deal it replaces.

The UK public sector is a major buyer of hyperscale cloud. The department’s notice, published on 30 October 2026 through the government’s Find a Tender service, sets an estimated budget of £881,621,007 excluding VAT, or about £1.1bn including VAT, for a contract that will run from December 2027 to December 2029.

A separate market-engagement notice covers the same procurement, with a formal contract notice expected in January 2027.

The £881.6m deal replaces the £450m contract AWS won in 2023, which had a three-year duration.

Because the Home Office packs a larger sum into a shorter term this time around, the implied annual commitment rises from about £150m to approximately £441m.

Transparency data compiled by BidSkim shows recorded Home Office payments to AWS rising from £48.4m in 2020 to £93.5m in 2024, then easing to £81.5m in 2025 and £51.5m in the first seven months of 2026. The total since January 2020 stands at £444.6m across 593 transactions.

Most of the money is booked to the department’s technology function. Spending under Digital Data and Technology (DDaT) totals £361.1m across 474 transactions, with a further £83.4m under COO – Home Office Digital – a switch that appears in the data from September 2025. Recorded payments peaked at £93.5m in 2024 and have not fallen below £81m in a full year since 2023.

The figures carry limits. They capture only transactions of more than £25,000, so they understate the true total, and with the proviso that contract value is a ceiling rather than a spending commitment. Recent annual payments of about £90m sit far below the £441m a year the new notice implies.

AWS in the UK public sector

AWS is one of the government’s 12 strategic technology suppliers, a group now dominated by foreign-owned firms after Capita became the last UK-headquartered name on the list.

Computer Weekly’s analysis of the UK’s £9bn public sector cloud spend found AWS winning contracts directly, while much of Microsoft Azure’s business runs through resellers.

Much AWS consumption is bought the same way, through partners rather than direct. Five resellers won one in seven UK public sector IT deals in 2025-26, which means direct-payment records such as BidSkim’s understate AWS’s real footprint in government.

The revolving door between Whitehall and big tech runs through AWS as well, with former officials moving between the department and the hyperscaler.

The £450m deal drew concerns when it was signed due to the scale of the commitment and the Home Office’s dependence on a single hyperscaler. The renewal extends that dependence for another two years from late 2027, at an annual rate that nearly trebles.

For a department that runs immigration, borders and policing systems on public cloud, exit costs are high and alternatives thin.

Before the January contract notice lands, the Home Office will run a market-engagement exercise. This is the formal chance to establish whether £881.6m is a maximum spend or a genuine expectation, and whether anyone other than AWS stands a realistic chance of winning.

The timing coincides with the current arrangement running towards its end as the department consolidates systems onto cloud, and as ministers press for more sovereign capability in public IT.

A renewal priced at nearly three times the annual rate of the deal that preceded it suggests AWS has become a default.

title: UK government ‘house of cards’ heavily reliant on US AI models
raw_text:
The artificial intelligence (AI) tools used by the UK government rely almost exclusively on models from US tech firms, raising questions over contingency planning.

According to a response to a freedom of information (FOI) request from UK AI firm Aventail, 10 of the 11 AI tools deployed or bought by the Cabinet Office use AI models developed by US tech firms.

While the models are hosted in the UK, the design, access and pricing are controlled by US organisations.  

Google, OpenAI, Microsoft or Anthropic are used directly or through Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services (AWS). The only exception is PolyAI, a UK company whose models are used for the government’s shared services provider, SSCL.

The Cabinet Office confirmed that Google Gemini is the primary authorised enterprise-level generative AI tool. Other AI tools used include Hansard AI for parliamentary and legislative research, Minute for creating meeting notes, and GCS Assist for government communications.

Joe Ward, CEO of Aventail, the company that made the FOI request, said: “Vital tools at the heart of government depend almost entirely on a handful of US companies. Hosting the data in the UK helps, but it does not change who controls the models, the pricing or the terms of access.”

He said he supported the UK government’s use of the latest US models, but added: “We risk building a house of cards if essential services depend on continued access to any one supplier. We need flexible infrastructure that lets public bodies switch providers, adopt new models and run open-weight alternatives under their own control when needed.”

Continuity question

The FOI request to the Home Office, which manages the government’s AI and technology supplier relationships, asked for details of any business continuity plans, risk assessments or risk register entries that address an outage of, or loss of access to, those providers’ services.

In response, the government said the information does exist, but that disclosing it would prejudice the prevention or detection of crime.

“The information contains details about the detection and prevention of crime which would assist criminals to plan and execute criminal acts and to avoid detection. Disclosure would thus make the prevention of certain crimes more difficult and reduce the effectiveness of the police service in detecting the perpetrators,” the Cabinet Office said in its response.

Mark Lewis, a specialist IT outsourcing lawyer at Stephenson Harwood, asked how the government thinks it can “ever extricate itself”.

“It’s not just that they’re all US, but there is a high concentration of the leading developers. Moreover, the infrastructure, of course, is inevitably US cloud,” said Lewis. “It’s all very well talking about sovereignty, but how realistic is it, given that proportion of dependency on not just a handful of US frontier AI labs, but also US cloud?”

He added that supplier lock-in is also a risk that could repeat what has happened in cloud computing: “AI labs locking in customers is exactly the same as we saw with the cloud.”

But Lewis added that the government could well have negated risks through the deals it signed. “What we don’t know, in fairness to the UK government, is whether they’ve managed to do smart commercial deals. But, bluntly, given what we know about UK government procurement – and in particular IT procurement – it’s hard to imagine that the UK government would be in a strong position. But we don’t know, in fairness.”
